This is was an odd situation that I observed with Brett Engstrom and which we discussed extensively. It's hard to see in photos but there is a distinct nest constructed, about .75 x 1 meters on the inside edge, from excavated peat and spruce boughs. There is evidence that the builder tried to burrow under a peat hummock around a larger spruce , perhaps trying to den undernearth it before realizing that it wasn't working out and creating the nest of broken boughs. We concluded that nothing but a bear could or would have made this structure but I'd like to hearing other ideas! I wonder how hibernating in a bog was and if they'll try it again or if it was a teenager learning an uncomfortable lesson?

remarks: Rangers were very excitedly trying to chase it down with a handheld large antenna (radiotagged bear?) Traffic was coming to a stop pointlessly since it was barely visible from the top of large boulders on the roadside. Some were scared even though from what I gather these are pretty much just overgrown racoons, unless you get on their wrong side in breeding season. Apparently a juvenile if the gossip I heard the next day was correct. Didn't seem to care at all about the clamor about it, the bear just stayed well within the meadow away from trails by >=50', head down looking for bulbs probably.
Best I could do with the DSLR and a 300mm lens (and lots of cropping). Pretty sure this is a cinnamon phase black bear, not a grizzly, but I am not 100% certain.

wood damage caught my attention from the road. I’ve noticed that it seems fairly common to find bear rub trees in eastern US forests and in the Rockies but in MN and WI I have seldom found them. However, since my awareness has been tuned to finding *what* they are scent marking on instead, if not trees, I have found bear rubs on many telephone poles and sign and fence posts. Pictured here can be seen incisor marks and chipping away of the wood from biting, as well as a great deal of bear hair essentially from 6-10 inches all the way to 5 feet up this pole. I pictured what I could see most easily on the camera.

I saw these two young bears playing in the woods, so I stopped to record some videos. Then they smelled me (before they saw me), stopped playing, and came toward me to investigate. One of the siblings (I assume) got a bit too close to me. So I walked away from them, but then they followed me as I continued my walk; one very close behind me, the other keeping a better distance. Whenever I turned and waved an arm or spoke loudly, the closer bear would momentarily back away, but then continue to follow me once I started walking again; just curiously and calmly following behind me. This went on for about ten minutes until I met up with my son, and while we were talking about the bears, they decided to wander off in a different direction. I hope they stay out of trouble...

remarks: This photo was taken Oct. 31, 2025 at a cow tank (like a small pond) roughly three-quarters of a mile south of Point of Pines Lake on the San Carlos Apache Reservation in Arizona. It’s pretty clear the animals are black bears, presumably a mother and cub. It’s worth noting that the photo was taken from a considerable distance, then heavily cropped (adorable as the bears were, I did not want to approach a protective mamma bear). When I first saw the bears they both had their heads in that blue barrel. Later I called the San Carlos Department of Recreation & Wildlife to ask about such barrels, which I noticed at a number of locations in the general vicinity of Point of Pines Lake. They said the barrels contain a nutritional supplement for cattle, which have been having a hard time due to recent drought. For whatever it’s worth, I also saw a mountain lion at the shore of Point of Pines Lake. However, it darted off before I could get a photo, so you’ll just have to take my word for it.

remarks: This black bear (Ursus americanus) was spotted near a small tributary stream to hemlock creek. The bear was walking the banks of the creek when spotted then walked to the top of the ridge line. You can tell this is a black bear by its dark black colored fur. The other factor you can use to tell this is a bear is the large size of the animal. We know it is a black bear considering the black bear is the only species of bear that inhabits this region. The temperature at the time of the sighting was 70f with a high of 74 and a low of 39. It was sunny with no perception and low humidity. There was almost no wind with a 2mph E wind. The bear was seen walking the edge of the stream our best guess was the bear was eating crayfish coming out of the stream bank because we observed this happen quite a few times this day. The bear was also following a path that had many deer tracks and scat. The bear could have been following the scent of the deer or just using the path.
Outside my Aunts house
Several places along the creek had tracks on the bank like the first photo. This site let it get to open water.

remarks: Android pic. Gif is from a longer video of the big bald black bear boldly biting bark.

I am always scanning for wildlife as I drive, in case something tries to cross the road for instance, and this bear easily caught my peripheral vision attention about 20 meters off the edge of PA State Route 22, north of Johnstown, about two hours from home. I pulled over immediately and walked back a little, to see if it was still there. I stayed about fifty meters away from it and took pictures. It seemed to want to cross the road, but turned back a couple times. It seemed to catch scent of me, and then clearly looked right at me, sitting back on its haunches. I have some experience with the Fish and Game Commission inspecting bear carcasses harvested by hunters, weighing and extracting a tooth for analysis etc., but this bear was noticeably bigger than any I have seen before. I would guess roughly in the 400 pound (180 kilogram) range. It was a bit scary actually to be looked at by such a huge animal. I did not see any cubs. That, along with its tremendous size suggests that this was a big male. It did not seem disturbed. It turned away from me calmly, and walked around a little for a couple minutes. It then went farther away, at one point standing up to get one more look at me (he was *towering* standing up), before actually laying down for ten minutes. He then got up slowly and walked away north into the woods. Another couple that stopped when they saw me with my camera said they had been seeing a bear with two cubs in the neighborhood lately, but that this one was much bigger. Wow. This was, for me, a very rare encounter with a literally awesome creature.

remarks: Finally got a clear view of what species has been leaving all that bear scat around. Young black bear paid us a visit. Looks like he is curious and was sniffing around. Have definitely seen signs of activity around and we have had bears get into stuff before, but never seen one on our deck. Got a call from the neighbor that one was headed down our driveway but he went over a fence. And then 15 min later he appeared on our deck. We spied him through the window from where we were eating dinner. Dog didn’t even notice. Bear was very quiet. Once I opened a window to yell and scare him, he ran quickly away. Just the sound of the window opening spooked him. So hopefully he continues to be scared. ;) He was probably in the vicinity becuase of the orchard nearby. Will be on the alert.

Bears are a rare sight in southwestern Pennsylvania and the panhandle of West Virginia, but steadily reported occasionally over the years. I did not set eyes on this lone individual, but its appearance in front of an unmanned automatic motion detecting night-vision wildlife monitoring camera is worth reporting for the benefit of the awareness of local residents, and the wildlife biologists with whom we share our observational data. For what it is worth, this Bear was headed west I believe, in the middle of the night, just a few days after the New Moon. Anecdotally, I have spoken to someone in the area that has seen Black Bears emerging from dens near a remote stretch of Buffalo Creek northwest of Taylorstown, 6-7 kilometers from here within the last ten years. This person later inspected the interior of the dens and reported seeing Bear hair and other signs of occupation. A brother of mine also saw a Black Bear by the large sandstone outcrop with Bear sized caves in it in the *Bear Rock Lakes Wildlife Management Area*, about 15 kilometers west of here, just into West Virginia. Neither of these sighting resulted in photographs or other "hard" evidence however. I'm told that Bears do not "live" here, but are seen occasionally as they travel through the area. If that is the case, where would they be travelling from - and to? If they live in the mountains to the east, then why do some end up here in the middle of the Allegheny Plateau? Having seen these huge Apex Omnivores more than once myself in the wild, I can attest to the awe that they can provoke when we are lucky enough to encounter them in their natural forest habitat. With proof that they are indeed sometimes "out there" even so close to home, it is exciting to anticipate and imagine where and when my next close encounter might be. I have been deliberately a little vague as to the location of this "trail-cam" observation, setting the uncertainty radius to 1.5 kilometers (though I know precisely where it took place somewhere within that radius) so that the landowner is not pestered by nosy enquiries or curious intruders. Enough time has passed to assure that this Bear is likely far away by now in any case. This landscape is characterized by rolling hills covered with second growth deciduous woodland, mixed with small cattle, dairy, and sheep farms.

A live spruce tree near the Sunrise Visitor Center on the east side of Mt. Rainier, Washington state, USA at about 6500 feet. Something ripped all the bark off. See dirty paw prints in photo 1. There were widely-spaced claw marks (couldn't tell if 4 or 5) and dirt around the barkless trunk, and it looked like possibly rodent chew marks around the trunk? Porcupines are extremely rare here and I'm not even sure these are actual chew marks, but I'd assume squirrels or something similar before porcupines. There was fresh bear scat on the trail a distance away. My guess is a bear tore the bark off for whatever reason and maybe a rodent chewed on the barkless trunk.
All appear very healthy. No signs of mange.

remarks: These are screenshots from video my coworker Brian shot. This Bear caused all kinds of a commotion when it wandered down from the mountains to Chatsworth, not a normal place to find a wandering bear. This video was shot, just before 4am, as the bear was looking for a place to get some sleep. As you can see her yawning in the pic. She climbed even higher in this tree and slept until around 8a. Then 4 hours later she came down, wandered around the gated parking lot and then climbed up a different tree. She was there a couple more hours, until Fish & Wildlife folks tranquillized her and gave her a free ride back home to the mountains. UPDATE - since this bear was all over the news, CA Fish and Wildlife has been sharing her GPS tracking data with the media- She is tagged, known as “Yellow 2291”. She is one of their most travel bears. She lives in Angeles national Forest. They said she traveled across the entire 210 foothill corridor, she went under the Newhall Pass, which is where the 5 and 14 freeways cross. She made it all the way to Malibu. They say she traveled at least 100 miles, crossing at least five different freeways. They believe her appearance in Chatsworth was her getting lost on her way home, back to the Angeles National Forest.
Had a radio collar, was being tracked with telemetry by some rangers
